text.p: Bayerische Hypotheken- und Wechsel-Bank AG said on Wednesday its first-quarter earnings were above plan and it was upbeat for 1997 after sustaining a fall in operating profit last year.

Germany's fifth-largest listed bank, a strong mortgage lender, said it had exceeded by far its own expectations for commission income in the first two months, while trading income was above target and interest income slightly below.
"Initial figures for March confirm the trend and the first quarter went quite well," chief executive Eberhard Martini told a news conference.
The bank was positive about 1997 as share prices were unlikely to fall dramatically, interest rates were set to remain stable this year and demand for mortgage loans was seen staying strong.

Martini also moved to dampen vague but persistent market speculation that Hypo-Bank might face a takeover bid, saying he could not seen any rival paying the price which could be as high as 20 billion marks ($12 billion) -- the market capitalisation of 14 billion plus a premium.
"I can't imagine that someone would pay this for a bank," he said, adding that the capitalisation of Germany's big banks had reached "unbelievable volumes".

But Martini said banks could not afford to ignore the merger speculation which has gripped the entire banking sector since last July, when market leader Deutsche Bank AG announced it had a 5.21 percent stake in Bayerische Vereinsbank AG.
Deutsche's move fuelled expectations of consolidation in Germany's overcrowded banking sector and Hypo-Bank shares were among the main gainers alongside Vereinsbank.
"We take this very seriously and try to be prepared for all constellations that may arise," Martini said. But there was no sign that any single investor was amassing a block of shares in his bank.
Hypo-Bank's shares closed down 0.90 marks at 55.40 marks after rising to a year's high of 58.50 marks earlier in the day on a renewed bout of takeover rumours.
Outlining last year's results, Martini said operating profit after risk provisions had fallen 8.7 percent to 1.19 billion marks, contrasting with hefty earnings gains at the bank's larger rivals.

The earnings drop was caused by a steep decline in income from securities held in its liquidity portfolio -- calculated as part of risk provisions under German accounting practices -- because the bank chose not to realise price gains.
As a result, net risk provisions surged 57.8 percent to 1.3 billion marks, but Martini said that overall the bank set aside slightly less for credit risks last year than in 1995.
The rise in net provisions helped to reduce Hypo-Bank's tax burden last year so that net income rose 5.7 percent to 714.9 million marks, Martini said.

Martini said administration costs rose by just 4.6 percent to 3.33 billion marks last year, helping to push the ratio of costs to income down to 57.1 percent. This was by far the lowest among top German banks which are struggling to rationalise their expensive domestic branch networks.
Strong demand for mortgage lending, fuelled by Germany's low interest rates, boosted net interest income by 7.3 percent to 4.4 billion marks.

Net commission income jumped 43.8 percent to 1.18 billion marks partly because of the first-time consolidation of British fund management Foreign & Colonial (F&C) in which Hypo-Bank increased its stake to 65 percent last year from 50 percent.
Income from own-account trading rose 15.6 percent to 222.1 million marks.

The F&C stake purchase and strong expansion in mortgage lending in late 1996 reduced Hypo-Bank's core capital ratio to 4.9 percent from 5.5 percent. Martini said he would not rule out a share issue this year, although there were no plans for such a move now.
The bank plans to issue profit participation certificates or warrant bonds this year to help beef up reserves. ($ = 1.716 German Marks)
